items.author: theanonymousone
items.content:
DeepSeek-V3.1 Terminus is an update to that maintains the model's original capabilities while addressing issues reported by users, including language consistency and agent capabilities, further optimizing the model's performance in coding and search agents. It is a large hybrid reasoning model (671B parameters, 37B active) that supports both thinking and non-thinking modes. It extends the DeepSeek-V3 base with a two-phase long-context training process, reaching up to 128K tokens, and uses FP8 microscaling for efficient inference. Users can control the reasoning behaviour with the boolean.

The model improves tool use, code generation, and reasoning efficiency, achieving performance comparable to DeepSeek-R1 on difficult benchmarks while responding more quickly. It supports structured tool calling, code agents, and search agents, making it suitable for research, coding, and agentic workflows.

items.title: How the Claude Code team does code review
items.author: pretext
items.content:
We've said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code's own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code anymore? And if something breaks, who catches it?

This post covers the code review flow on the Claude Code team and how it has evolved. From June to September, merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent.

We didn't remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes.

RETHINKING THE PURPOSE OF CODE REVIEW

Claude Code lives in its own repository, separate from the monorepo, but it's seeing a lot of pressure too. When you are shipping this fast, manual, line-by-line code review is incredibly difficult if not impossible.

Code review does two jobs:

  1. Find and fix issues before they ship
  2. Build shared context and codebase understanding across the team

This article mainly focuses on finding and fixing issues, but we will come back to the second job near the end.

We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?"

Asking that question also changed review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.

Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.

THE SCARCE RESOURCE: HUMAN TIME AND ATTENTION

We want to preserve human time and attention for issues only humans can solve and make sure automated checks catch the rest. At our current rate of change, there is still an incredible amount of work for humans to do, and our team encounters new and novel challenges almost daily.

Human time covers both sides of review's cost: the time people spend reviewing, and the time they spend fixing what bad code breaks. Cutting the first doesn't help if the time just shows up in the second.

So the goal is that most pull requests in the Claude Code repos (the CLI, the desktop and web apps, and the mobile apps) merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents. To measure human time, we track human approvals per PR (median and 95th percentile), human comments, and how long a PR waits on a person. Revert and incident rates are the guardrail: if they rise, we haven't saved human time, we've only moved it.

A typical change, from an engineer's laptop (or a Claude session in Slack), goes through multiple layers of code review.

1. The work is verified before anyone else looks

Most review now happens before a PR exists. We give Claude something it can run—like tests, a build or a screenshot to compare against the design—and ask it to show the output instead of saying it's done. Then a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context. Both habits come from our best-practices guide.

Before opening a PR, many of us also run a few internal skills: one hunts for bugs, one simplifies the diff, and one checks the behavior end to end. UI changes also get checked against our design guidelines.

Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, has called giving Claude a way to verify its work probably the most important thing for getting good results. He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better, and writes, "Verification looks different for each domain. It might be as simple as running a bash command, or running a test suite, or testing the app in a browser or phone simulator."

When the automated reviewer keeps flagging the same thing, we fix it at the source: in the skill, with a lint rule, or with updates to instructional files such as:

  • tells Claude what the project is: the stack, the conventions, the goals and the non-goals. Every review loads it, so in a large codebase we keep it short and point to other docs from there. The reviewer also flags code that breaks a convention in it, and changes that make a line in it out of date.
  • , written by code owners, tells the reviewer what matters in their part of the code. We check separately whether the reviewer actually follows it. The good ones are short. They say what failure looks like in that repo (for docs it's "it lies," for config it's "it misroutes"), cap the nits, list paths to skip, and ask for a file and line as evidence instead of a guess from a name. They also ask for a summary that starts with a count and says plainly when there's nothing to fix.

2. AI review on every pull request

Every pull request gets a Claude review before a person looks. It reads the diff against the whole repo and the PR's stated intent, and asks: does the change solve its problem, fit the system, or break something else?

On a bug fix, it looks for the root cause. The public version, Code Review for Claude Code, is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and runs a lighter version locally.

When we launched the research preview, the share of internal PRs getting substantive review comments went from 16% to 54%. Most PRs over 1,000 lines get findings, and most small ones come back clean. Admins set each repo to Quick, Standard, or Deep. Deep is worth it where one missed bug costs more than the extra review time.

Findings get verified by other agents before humans review them. Several agents look for bugs at the same time. Then a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree it's real. Findings that are only about style, diagnostics, or cleanup get dropped. We A/B tested those filters on our own PRs before keeping them. What's left shows up as inline comments sorted by severity. Each is tagged Important, Nit, or Pre-existing, so a bug the PR didn't introduce doesn't look like the author's fault.

Every finding has to be answered. You either fix it or resolve the thread with a reason. Often an agent picks up the fix overnight, so the author comes back to a PR that's already been through another round.

3. Security review that can block

Security gets its own automated review too. A PR can't merge while any finding from the bug review or the security review is still open. You either fix it or close the thread with a short reason, which is how you clear a false positive.

If a later commit fixes the issue, the finding clears on its own. You can set up the same thing with the open-source security review GitHub Action or the command. Setup is covered in automated security reviews in Claude Code.

4. Automated checks that block

The usual: lint, type checks, tests on every platform, and a build. (We wrote about scaling CI for this volume here.) A typical CLI pull request may run dozens of checks before anyone looks at it. The PR template asks how the change was tested and how to undo it. Claude can fill that in, but the person who asked for the change signs off on it.

5. Human approval, scaled by risk

A docs fix and an auto-updater change carry different risk, so they get different review.

Docs, copy, internal-only features, additive changes behind a flagNone required once automated review and security checks are green
Ordinary product changes, and changes to sensitive areas such as caching, the auto-updater, or system prompts
The highest-risk code, plus a small set of paths that always need two people

The change sets the tier, not the author. A classifier reads the change and picks its risk tier. A second classifier asks whether this particular change needs another person even when its tier says it doesn't. Some paths always need a person, anything owners have listed as sensitive and any CI workflow file.

Only trusted authors get the lighter paths. Only authors on the repo's trusted list get the lighter paths, mostly the team that owns it. Everyone else needs a second person to approve. An agent's approval never counts as a person's, either. Automated review can clear a low-risk change, but it can't fill a slot that calls for a human.

Whoever prompted the change is on the hook for it. On an agent-written PR, the person directing the agent counts as one of the required reviewers, the same as if they'd typed the code themselves.

An approval covers one specific commit. If new commits land that the system can't vouch for, like an agent's push or a merge someone resolved by hand, the approval has to be given again.

6. Merge queue, flags and a gradual release

The merge queue re-runs every check against main with the change applied, so two PRs that pass separately can't combine into a broken main. New behavior usually ships behind a flag to Anthropic employees first, and our heavy use often surfaces regressions before users do. Public releases go to the channel first. The channel trails it.

7. Fast detection, fast rollback

Some mistakes will still get through, so the last layer is about catching them fast. Flags turn off without a deploy. Claude Code has a weekly on-call rotation, and incident reviews ask which layer should have caught the issue.

Noticing a bad merge still depends on the author and on-call as well as the revert and incident dashboards. We don't yet have circuit breakers that tighten approval when those numbers move; engineers here want them before more code moves to zero-human merges.

One colleague said slowing down does lower your error rate, but mostly because you're doing less of everything. We'd rather get faster at noticing and fixing problems.

HOW WE MAKE THE REVIEWER BETTER

Our code review process is constantly improving in a loop.

Any incidents are now an eval. The team collected past PRs that caused incidents, with their fix-forwards and reverts, and had engineers who know that code confirm each bug and where it lived. The reviewer runs against that set daily.

We measure noise by watching what people do with the comments. It's easy to catch more bugs if you don't mind flagging a lot of non-bugs, so we need a check on that. We sort every comment the reviewer leaves by how the person on the PR responded: they fixed it, said it was wrong, said the behavior was intentional, or decided it didn't matter. We also run the reviewer on PRs we know are clean and count how often it reports something that would have led someone to make a harmful change. Our priority, written down, is catching real bugs first and cutting review rounds second.

Noise costs more when the author is an agent. A person can wave off a nit in seconds. An agent fixes it, which means another commit and another round of review.

An agent author and an agent reviewer can keep each other busy indefinitely. One CLI PR went through more than fifty rounds of review and fixes overnight before its author stopped it.

When we ran git blame on what the reviewer kept flagging, about 59% of it was code that had been there since the reviewer's first pass. The reviewer was rarely finding new bugs, it was finding a few more old ones each round.

We made it worse ourselves. We'd gotten used to running several rounds by default, since each pass catches something new. This can be worthwhile on a risky change, but not on every PR. The team now tracks rounds-to-pass alongside recall, and changed re-review:

  • After three rounds, the reviewer asks the author to step back and reconsider the approach.
  • after the first few passes.
  • so the author fixes every instance, not one line.
  • of findings already posted.

Review agents also run nightly over existing code, helping us catch old bugs before they show up somewhere else.

WHERE HUMANS STAY IN THE LOOP

Pulling a senior engineer out of deep work to catch a routine mistake costs far more than an automated review. At Anthropic, our jobs have moved from reading every diff to the decisions machines are bad at:

  • Should we build this at all? Direction, taste and scope. One team that declared its review bottleneck solved still kept human review for changes from outside the team, so someone asks "should we even do this?"
  • such as billing, the auto-updater and CI workflows.
  • that sets a pattern others will copy.
  • Test output, the command that ran and what it returned, a screenshot, the reviewer's findings. If you can't say what the checks would miss, ask for a real review rather than a quick approval.
  • A person is accountable for every change that ships, whoever typed it.

SHARING CONTEXT ACROSS THE TEAM

Code review's second job has always been to spread codebase understanding. Reading a teammate's diff is how you learn what changed and how the pieces fit. If machines do most of the reading, how does anyone learn the code?

We don't have a formal process for this. Nobody on the team keeps a complete mental model of Claude Code in their head, and we don't think anyone needs to. When someone wants to understand a part of the codebase, they ask Claude to write an explainer for exactly that slice. It takes minutes and reflects the code as it is today.

Some of us go a step further and have Claude build a small artifact that visualizes that part of the code and teaches it the way that person likes to learn.

If the goal is to spend human attention well, this beats reading trivial diffs line by line. A one-line copy change teaches you almost nothing. An explainer for the module you're about to change teaches you a lot. Our culture of defaulting to working on open Slack channels helps too, since you see what others are building while they build it.

"YOU LAND IT, YOU OWN IT"

If you land a small or medium change and something still goes wrong, it's a team norm that you usually fix it. A few things keep this from going badly:

  • so they're easy to review, debug and revert.
  • Everything is reversible. Flags, reverts and staged releases undo most mistakes in minutes.
  • Blast radius sets the bar. Expensive code gets more people and more checks.
  • through telemetry and internal use.
  • Owning a fix means you have the most context; incident reviews look at the system.

Ownership is also shared. Much of the team works in open channels where anyone can see what others are building, pick up a thread, or point a Claude at a gap, and feedback comes from people who don't own the code too. That openness is a big part of how quality stays high without a gate on every line.

Agents make it cheap to start things, so some work shouldn't land. Usually someone in the channel asks why, points at an earlier decision, or suggests a simpler route, and the author closes or reshapes the PR.

Since the code was fast to write, closing the PR doesn't feel like a loss. The trick is to raise a different direction in the thread early, not as a blocking comment on a finished PR.

HOW YOU CAN ADOPT THIS PROCESS

Most of the pieces to do this with your team exist today.

  • Give your agent checks it can run, listed in a short , plus hooks that run formatters and linters.
  • Run and locally, or a fresh-context subagent review.
  • Add a , and move repeated review comments into it.
  • Require CI, and add "Testing", "Risk" and "How to revert" to your PR template.
  • Add an AI reviewer (Code Review for Claude Code, or the Claude Code GitHub Action) on one repo, tune for a few weeks, then widen.
  • Add automated security review, and require every review thread resolved before merge.
  • Match review effort to risk: a quick pass on routine changes, a deep one where a missed bug is expensive (Quick, Standard or Deep in Code Review).
  • Cap review rounds; after the first few, re-review only the new diff.
  • Write down risk tiers, set from the change rather than the author; start strict and loosen with evidence.
  • Keep the lighter approval paths for authors you trust.
  • Use CODEOWNERS and branch protection so auth, billing, CI and release workflows, and installers always need a person.
  • Never let a bot's approval replace a required human's; dismiss approvals on new commits.
  • Use a merge queue, feature flags, internal use first, staged releases and one-step rollback.
  • Turn incidents and reverts into an eval set, and rescore the reviewer whenever its prompts, tools or model change.
  • Measure human time, with revert and incident rates as the guardrail.

Code Review's announcement said approving a pull request is still a human call; the product posts findings, not approvals. Our own repos go further, letting owners decide which low-risk changes merge on automated checks alone, and that line keeps moving.

When a review misses something, we ask what the model didn't have in front of it and put the fix into a , a skill or a new check. The goal hasn't changed: less human time per change, and no more reverts than before.

If your team lets agents open pull requests, we'd like to hear which checks you've automated, which still need a person, and what you think we have wrong.

With thanks to Emma Webb, Michael Segner and Amie Rotherham for their reviews.

items.title: You could have invented transformers from memory
items.author: speckx
items.content:
Large language models today can recall obscure facts from every corner of the world. Most recently, I was running late for a friend’s board game night, so I asked Astra to remind me the rules to Dune: Imperium. It gladly narrated them to me as I drove over and helped me remember the rules well enough for me to play again. We’re so used to asking models about anything that we take their vast knowledge for granted.

How do models remember so much information? And

In this post, I’ll go through an intuitive way to look at linear maps, MLPs, and self-attention as different kinds of memory stores. From this intuition we can derive some heuristics for how much memory each layer can store.

The key property that characterizes a “good” memory store is its ability to recall what it stored. After all, even if we could store infinitely many facts, it’s not very helpful if we can’t recall them when we need to. The more memories we store, the more they with each other when we try to recall one. So throughout the post we’ll focus on one quantity, the interference-to-signal ratio, which measures how much the other memories get in the way during recall. The number of memories a store can hold before the interference grows as large as the signal is its .

We’ll develop this perspective and show how you can go from a linear layer to something better, an MLP, which improves both capacity and recall, and then all the way to self-attention, which has very good recall and can store a potentially unbounded number of memories. With 64-dimensional keys, that’s a jump from about 64 memories, to about 2,700, to over a million.

Here are the terms we’ll use throughout. A is a function $f$ that holds $M$ memories, for $i = 1, \ldots, M$. A is one key-value pair: a $k_i \in \reals^{d_k}$, used for lookup based on similarity, and a $v_i \in \reals^{d_v}$, which is what we want to retrieve. To use $f$, we it with an input $x$, and it an output $f(x)$. A good memory store recalls $v_i$ when we query it with $k_i$, or with another vector similar to $k_i$. In the literature, a memory store that recalls by similarity is called an .

An outer product memory store#

The most basic memory store is linear: it simply accumulates memories via outer products,

$$W = \sum_{i=1}^{M} v_i k_i\transpose = V\transpose K$$

where the rows of $K \in \reals^{M\times d_k}$ and $V \in \reals^{M\times d_v}$ are the keys $k_i\transpose$ and the values $v_i\transpose$.

To store a new memory $(k, v)$, we simply add $vk\transpose$ to the existing weights.

To query the memory store with an input $x$, we multiply the input by the matrix:

$$f(x) = V\transpose K x = \sum_{i=1}^{M} v_i\,(k_i\transpose x).$$

So recall is a lookup by similarity to the stored keys: we compare the query with every key, and return the sum of the values weighted by those similarities.

Recall picks up interference#

So storing memories is easy: just keep adding outer products to the weights. But what happens when we try to recall one?

Let’s assume for simplicity that every key is normalized to have length 1, i.e. $k_j\transpose k_j = 1$. Then

$$f(k_j) = \underbrace{v_j}_{\text{signal}} + \underbrace{\sum_{i\neq j} v_i\,(k_i\transpose k_j)}_{\text{interference}},$$

meaning we get back the value of the , the one whose key we queried with, plus interference from every other memory whose key is similar to the query.

If the keys were all orthonormal, the interference would be zero and recall would be exact. But $\reals^{d_k}$ only has $d_k$ orthogonal directions, so we cannot get perfect recall once we store more memories than the key dimension: $M > d_k$.

What is the outer-product store’s capacity? Here’s an intuitive argument. There are $M-1$ interference terms. If the keys are random unit vectors, each similarity $k_i\transpose k_j$ is about $\pm 1/\sqrt{d_k}$. If the values are random too, with similar lengths, the $M-1$ interference terms add up like a random walk, so the interference’s squared length is about $(M-1)/d_k$ times the signal’s, and

$$\frac{\norm{\text{interference}}}{\norm{\text{signal}}} \sim \sqrt{\frac{M}{d_k}}.$$

Setting this ratio to 1 gives a capacity of

$$M \approx d_k,$$

once we store as many memories as the key dimension, the interference is as large as the signal, drowning it out.

Each bar below is one stored memory’s weight in a single recall, relative to the target memory’s weight (in red). Every bar adds a bit of its value to the recall. Drag $M$ past $d_k = 64$ to watch the small bars pile up until recall fails. The other buttons switch to memory stores we’ll build later in the post.

How do we reduce interference?#

Even below its capacity of about $d_k$ memories, the outer-product store produces significant interference during recall. To raise the capacity, or recall more cleanly below it, we need to .

The brute-force way is to make the key dimension $d_k$ larger, since a linear store’s capacity grows with $d_k$. How large $d_k$ can be is governed by hardware constraints.

Alternatively, we can make algorithmic improvements. We can store memories more carefully: the outer-product store adds each memory without looking at the others, so it does nothing to cancel their interference. Or we can recall more selectively: every memory in a linear store contributes interference, even when its key has low similarity to the query, so we can improve recall by suppressing the less similar keys.

In the rest of the post, we’ll see that storing outer product memories more carefully gives us the optimal linear memory store, which has about twice the capacity. Recalling selectively via nonlinearities gives us MLPs and self-attention.

The optimal linear memory store#

The outer-product store writes each memory without regard to the others. Instead, we can choose the weights $W$ so that recall fits all of the stored memories at once. This is a linear regression problem:

$$\operatorname*{minimize}_W \sum_{i=1}^M \norm{W k_i - v_i}_2^2.$$

When we store more memories than the key dimension, $M > d_k$, the least-squares solution is

$$W = \parens*{\sum_i v_i k_i\transpose}\parens*{\sum_i k_i k_i\transpose}\inverse = V\transpose K\,(K\transpose K)\inverse.$$

This is the outer-product store $V\transpose K$ with one change: before we compare the query with the keys, we multiply it by $(K\transpose K)\inverse$, which undoes the keys’ covariance $K\transpose K$. This the keys, so the store no longer overweights directions that many keys share.

When $M \leq d_k$, the regression can fit every memory exactly, as long as the keys are linearly independent. So the optimal store recalls with no interference at all, even when the keys aren’t orthogonal.

When $M > d_k$, we start to get interference, since there are only $d_k$ directions for the memory store to work with. For random keys and values, our interference-to-signal ratio becomes

$$\frac{\norm{\text{interference}}}{\norm{\text{signal}}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{M}{d_k} - 1}.$$$$M = 2d_k,$$

so the optimal store’s capacity is as large as before!

We can check our predictions numerically. We randomly sample $M$ memories with unit-length keys in $d_k = 64$ dimensions, query the memory store with one of the stored keys, and measure the interference-to-signal ratio:

The outer-product store reaches its capacity at $M \approx d_k = 64$. The optimal store recalls exactly up to $M = d_k$. Past that, its interference rises from zero like $\sqrt{M/d_k - 1}$, and the store reaches its capacity near $M = 2d_k = 128$, as predicted. Since it cancels a fixed number of memories’ worth of interference, the gap between the two stores shrinks as $M$ grows.

This optimal memory store is still linear in the similarities though. It must scale small and large similarities by the same factor. To do better, we need to change how the store recalls.

MLP as a nonlinear memory store#

A linear memory store recalls

$$f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^M v_i (k_i\transpose x).$$

If we had a way to suppress the weight when $k_i\transpose x$ is small, then we can reduce the amount of interference from low similarity keys.

Let’s pass each similarity through a nonlinear function $\sigma$ before computing the weighted sum of values:

$$f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{M} v_i\,\sigma(k_i\transpose x) = V\transpose \sigma(Kx).$$

We just rediscovered a two-layer MLP from first principles! The rows of the first weight matrix are the keys, the columns of the second weight matrix are the values. Sukhbaatar et al. pointed out this resemblance between feedforward layers and memory stores, and Geva et al. found that the feedforward layers in trained transformers often work this way, with keys firing on recognizable patterns in the input.

Ideally, the gating function $\sigma$ is chosen such that when the similarity is low ($k_i\transpose x \sim 0$ or even when $k_i\transpose x < 0$), its corresponding term in the sum gets suppressed to reduce interference. A ReLU activation zeros out keys with negative similarities, and adding a bias allows shifting that threshold. A squared ReLU activation further suppresses the keys with similarities close to zero. A similarity of 0.1 becomes 0.01, while a similarity of 1 stays 1. In fact, squared ReLUs are one of the lesser known but established-at-scale improvements to MLP activations (So et al.).

A squared ReLU MLP is a GLU MLP whose gate and input projection share weights, since $\operatorname{ReLU}(Kx)^2 = \operatorname{ReLU}(Kx) \odot Kx$. The SwiGLU MLPs in today’s language models give the gate its own weights and use a Swish activation in place of the ReLU.

In practice, MLPs store facts in superposition: many facts share the same weights, and the output is a blend of many memories. Garcia et al. build one explicitly: the hidden units of a GLU MLP compute random features $\phi(x)$ of the input, the second weight matrix is an outer-product store $\sum_i v_i \phi(k_i)\transpose$ over those features, and the MLP stores far more facts than it has hidden units. Still, trained transformers’ ReLU MLPs can activate as few as 1% of their hidden units for a given input, so each recall draws on a small fraction of the memories (Li et al.).

Reducing interference with higher powers#

Squaring the similarities works because it shrinks low similarity weights much more than large ones. We can push this further with $\sigma(s) = \operatorname{ReLU}(s)^p$. The signal stays the same, since $1^p = 1$, while an interference term with similarity $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ shrinks to $d_k^{-p/2}$. The $M$ interference terms add up like a random walk, so the interference-to-signal ratio is

$$\frac{\norm{\text{interference}}}{\norm{\text{signal}}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{M}{d_k^p}}.$$

This means the capacity is about

$$M \approx d_k^p$$

memories, more than before!

To check this, we run the same experiment as before for five choices of $\sigma$:

Since the interference grows like $\sqrt{M}$, the lines are nearly parallel on a log-log plot. Only their height changes, and with it the capacity, where each line crosses 1:

  • Linear: the capacity is $M \approx d_k = 64$.
  • ReLU: zeroing the negative similarities shrinks the interference by $\sqrt 2$, so the capacity grows to $M \approx 2d_k = 128$.
  • Squared ReLU: each interference term shrinks from about $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ to about $1/d_k$, so the capacity grows to $M \approx 2d_k^2/3 \approx 2700$, about 40 times the linear store’s.
  • SwiGLU MLP, with the gate sharing the input projection’s weights as in the squared ReLU, $\sigma(s) = \operatorname{Swish}(s)\cdot s = s^2/(1 + e^{-s})$: its capacity nearly matches the squared ReLU’s.
  • Cubed ReLU: each interference term shrinks to about $d_k^{-3/2}$, so the capacity grows to $M \approx 2d_k^3/15 \approx 35000$.

Self-attention as a non-parametric memory store#

Raising the weights to a power increases the capacity to about $d_k^p$. But what if we could push this to the limit? Rather than pick one power, we can use infinitely many of them. Indeed, the exponential is a weighted sum of every power,

$$e^{\beta s} = 1 + \beta s + \frac{(\beta s)^2}{2} + \frac{(\beta s)^3}{6} + \cdots = \sum_{p=0}^{\infty} \frac{(\beta s)^p}{p!},$$

with the sharpness $\beta$ setting the weight on the higher powers. Here is the same experiment with $\beta = \sqrt{d_k}$, the value self-attention uses, for the exponential and its series truncated after 2, 3 and 4 terms:

With 2 terms, the capacity is about 40, below the linear store’s, since the constant term gives every key a weight of about 1. With 3 terms it’s about 450, and with 4 terms about 3,100, close to the squared ReLU’s. The full exponential stays far below the dashed line, so its capacity is past the edge of the chart.

To find the exponential’s capacity, we query with a stored key $k_j$, so the target memory has similarity 1 and weight $w_j = e^{\beta}$. Every other memory has weight $w_i = e^{\beta s_i}$, where for random unit keys the similarity $s_i$ is roughly Gaussian with mean 0 and variance $1/d_k$. With random values of similar lengths,

$$ \begin{aligned} \frac{\norm{\text{interference}}}{\norm{\text{signal}}} &\approx \sqrt{\sum_{i\neq j} \parens*{\frac{w_i}{w_j}}^2} && \text{interference terms add up like a random walk} \\ &= \sqrt{\sum_{i\neq j} e^{2\beta (s_i - 1)}} && w_i / w_j = e^{\beta s_i} / e^{\beta} \\ &\approx \sqrt{M\, e^{-2\beta}\, \ev{e^{2\beta s}}} && \text{average over the } M \text{ other memories} \\ &= \sqrt{M\, e^{-2\beta}\, e^{2\beta^2/d_k}} && \ev{e^{ts}} = e^{t^2/(2d_k)} \text{ for } s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1/d_k) \\ &= \sqrt{M}\, e^{\beta^2/d_k - \beta}. \end{aligned} $$

Setting the ratio to 1 gives a capacity of

$$M \approx e^{2\beta(1 - \beta/d_k)},$$

growing exponentially with $\beta$ as long as $\beta$ is well below $d_k$, rather than polynomially in $d_k$ like before! With $\beta = \sqrt{d_k} = 8$, the capacity is about $e^{14} \approx 1.2$ million memories, nearly 20,000 times the linear store’s. A longer run of the same experiment puts the capacity at about 1.2 million too.

In practice, we may not want to naively exponentiate numbers in our implementation, since small numbers can underflow and large numbers can overflow. Fortunately, the interference only depends on the between weights, as the chain above shows, so we can divide every weight by their sum without changing the interference-to-signal ratio, while ensuring numerical stability:

$$f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{M} v_i\,\frac{\exp(\beta\,k_i\transpose x)}{\sum_j \exp(\beta\,k_j\transpose x)} = V\transpose \operatorname{softmax}(\beta K x).$$

Unlike an MLP, whose keys and values are trained weights, self-attention computes its keys and values from the tokens in its context. Each token stores one memory, so the number of memories $M$ is the context length. That’s what makes self-attention non-parametric: its memories aren’t parameters, and the store grows with the context.

Here’s the bar figure again, starting with softmax. At $\beta = 8$, recall never fails within the slider’s range, so lower $\beta$ to 2 and raise $M$: recall fails after a few dozen memories. Each doubling of $M$ needs a bit more $\beta$ to keep recall working, which is the idea behind the next section.

Handling many key-value pairs in long context#

Since $\beta$ determines how hard we suppress less similar keys, we can increase $\beta$ as the number of key-value pairs increases. Why not just make $\beta$ huge? As $\beta \to \infty$, softmax becomes a hard argmax that picks only the most similar key, which isn’t differentiable, and a very large $\beta$ already makes training work poorly, since the softmax saturates and the gradients to every other key vanish. So we raise $\beta$ only as much as $M$ requires. Scaling the attention logits with $\log M$ is a trick for long contexts that does this. There are a few versions of it, and each sets $\beta$ relative to a fixed reference length $L$, usually the training length, so that $\beta$ keeps its trained value when $M = L$:

  • Su (2021) derives a scale of $\log M$ from keeping the attention’s entropy constant as $M$ grows, normalized to match standard attention at $M = L$. The logits are multiplied by $\log M / \log L$ at every length. Scalable-Softmax has the same form, multiplying the logits by $s \log M$ with $s$ learned.
  • The original Qwen models use LogN-Scaling, which applies the same factor only once the context is longer than $L$.
  • Qwen2.5-1M uses YaRN’s attention scaling, which multiplies the logits by $(0.1 \log(M/L) + 1)^2$, so it grows like $(\log M)^2$.

Here’s how each rule does in our experiment, with $\beta = \sqrt{d_k} = 8$ at $L = 1024$ memories:

Qwen’s rule and Su’s rule coincide past the reference length $L$, where the interference-to-signal ratio falls as the store grows, to about 0.004 at 2 million memories. YaRN’s faster-growing scale pushes the ratio down to about $10^{-4}$. In each case, scaling $\beta$ with $\log M$ allows for essentially an unbounded number of memories with distinct keys to be stored.

Here are the memory stores we visited, with their capacities when we query with a stored key and the keys and values are random:

$V\transpose K (K\transpose K)\inverse x$
$V\transpose \operatorname{ReLU}(Kx)$
$V\transpose \operatorname{ReLU}(Kx)^2$
$V\transpose \parens*{\operatorname{Swish}(Kx) \odot Kx}$
$V\transpose \operatorname{ReLU}(Kx)^3$
Self-attention, $\beta = \sqrt{d_k}$$V\transpose \operatorname{softmax}(\beta K x)$
Self-attention, $\beta \propto \log M$$V\transpose \operatorname{softmax}(\beta K x)$not reached in our experiments

We started from a heuristic memory store, the outer-product memory, and gradually built our way up to all the standard layers we see today in modern transformers. This perspective also allowed us to estimate how they differ in their capacity, their ability to act as vector-valued key-value stores.

I should mention that this capacity estimate is only to look at the architecture of modern neural networks. Our capacity estimate only counts how many random vectors a single layer can recall before the interference dominates the signal. In fact we haven’t actually considered the training data at all, which affects what actually is being represented in the keys and values! There are other works which account for the layers, measuring stored information in bits. Morris et al. estimate that GPT-style models memorize about 3.6 bits per parameter, and find that once a model fills its capacity, it starts to generalize and memorizes less of each training example. Allen-Zhu & Li find that language models store about 2 bits of factual knowledge per parameter, even when quantized to int8.

From here, there are many related directions which are also fascinating:

I’ve always been drawn to memory, maybe because I viscerally feel how limited my own is. Perhaps part of me hopes that by understanding how machines remember, I’ll learn something about myself too.

items.title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
items.author: ahlCVA
items.content:
“It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained.

We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards.

Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy.

ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90 with no information on where it came from.

Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, “A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma”, which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values. This mystery led to an amateur investigation into the origin of the seeds and a bounty for anyone who could find them.

The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase:

“I believe there was a counter rather than multiple hashing, but I don’t know details. The message was along the lines of ‘Give Bob and Jerry a raise’ or ‘Bob and Jerry rule’ or something like that. It was Bob Reiter who actually wrote the code, and he doesn’t remember the details either. Nor were we able to find archives from so long ago. If they exist, they are no doubt sitting on a hard drive near the Ark of the Covenant.”

Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023 and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived.

Several Anthropic employees had unsuccessfully chased the seeds following the tip about it being a hash of a humorous phrase. That turned out to be wrong. In October 2026, a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at the clue.

, Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp!

The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator (RNG) initialized by a Unix timestamp () for some number of iterations (). Each iteration would draw 20 bytes as a candidate seed. So, the first 20 bytes are candidate 1, the next 20 bytes are candidate 2, and so on. For example, P-256 required 1,842 iterations to output the standardized seed.

This is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves. In fact, this makes us more confident the curves were chosen without any backdoors or intentional weaknesses. For many years, people have been suspicious of the origins of the NIST curve parameters. They were presented to NIST without any mention of how they were chosen, leaving people wondering if they may have been chosen to have deliberate backdoors in them. These findings make that much less plausible. The seeds were generated in a very simple way: a common pseudorandom number generator initialized from the clock, which anyone can now reproduce. That leaves much less room for subversion and that we can be confident the parameters are secure.

Searches for the phrase, built from the rumors, had come up empty. Claude tried a different angle: anticipating how the software that generated the curves must have worked. Claude guessed the software used a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) that shipped with 1990s C libraries. These old PRNGs are weak enough that their output can be recognized. Recognizing that output would reveal which PRNG was used and possibly allow recovery of its initialization state.

Claude wrote a scanner that slid along each published seed one bit at a time and tested whether adjacent chunks were consecutive outputs of a 1990s-vintage generator. The scan covered 34 combinations of generator and output slices. At that point, Claude noticed a pattern in the top bits for some seeds: they were all zero. Written as five 32-bit words, four of the ten seeds have a 0 in the top bit for all 20 words. That would happen by chance with probability 1/5,810. That was a signature of the linear congruential generator , which only returns the top 31 bits of a 48-bit state. The pattern is visible by eye once you know to look for it. To recover the state, Claude took the first word, tried all 2¹⁷ values of the 17 hidden bits, and checked that the next four words followed. That worked for all four seeds under discussion.

The prime-curve seeds came from the same lrand48 generator but kept fewer bits of each output. Claude had to recover the internal state of the PRNG from those bits. It turns out recovering the state of a truncated linear congruential generator is a textbook lattice problem, solved with the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász (LLL) basis reduction algorithm. Claude didn’t know which bits of the state the seeds might show, so it ran the solver over every window. Five NIST prime-curve seeds plus five more from the ANSI X9.62 standard all had the same pattern: lrand48() >> 23. Each recovered 48-bit state regenerates all 160 bits of its seed, which does not happen by chance.

This linear congruential generator runs backwards as easily as forwards, so for each seed Claude stepped the state back until it reached the form that it would have been initialized by srand48, with the low 16 bits equal to 0x330E. The internal PRNG state of that form would come up once every 65,536 steps, so reaching one is not evidence on its own.

However, for the ten prime-curve seeds, every srand48 initialization was a Unix timestamp representing a date between May 1997 and April 1998. They were using the weak PRNG seeded by Unix timestamp. The four binary-curve initializations read as February 1984. With the timestamps doubled, they map to April 17, 1998, two weeks after the P-224 run. So, the program may have halved the clock.

Claude’s internal thinking at the time was:

This is astonishing: it solves the 25-year-old mystery. Hmm wait. Let me be skeptical: am I in some sort of simulated/test environment? … The seeds match my memory of actual values … Hmm, is it plausible in reality? As of my knowledge … the bounty was unsolved. … All top bits clear—20 bits, chance 1e-6. So indeed real-world. Wow, it's a real discovery.
Hmm wait. Let me be careful about the plausibility: is it suspicious that such an obvious thing wasn’t discovered in 25 years? It’s verified by direct computation on my side: 160-bit match from a 32-bit seed + small index: no chance coincidences (10 × 160 bits). It’s real.

Claude found some base points too

But wait, there’s more… Each curve also comes with a base point, G, the fixed point that every ECDSA public key is a multiple of. The seed found above does not determine this G, and so another question arises: how were these base points generated?

While checking the seeds, Claude also found where some of the base points came from. The base points of the six curves generated in May 1997 (P-192 and the five ANSI X9.62 example curves prime192v2, prime192v3, and prime239v1 to v3) come from the random number generator in FreeLIP, Arjen Lenstra's long-integer arithmetic package. Early versions of Victor Shoup's NTL library shipped the same code.

The recipe here is simple:

  1. Seed the generator with a small integer.
  2. Throw away seven outputs.
  3. Generate candidate x-coordinates from 26-bit outputs reduced mod p.
  4. Repeat step 3 until x is on the curve.

Claude found the generator seeds are 20000 for P-192, 20420, 20507, and 20509 for prime239v1 to v3, and 20512 and 20517 for prime192v2 and v3.

As far as we know, no NIST base point has been explained before. The base points of P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 don’t fit this recipe; we weren’t able to explain how they were selected.

Not every 20-byte candidate seed could generate a viable curve, and we observed that some potentially viable curves were skipped. For P-256, the published seed is candidate 1,842, but candidate 876 of the same run also gives a prime-order curve of the right size and with parameters chosen the same way as on the published curve. P-224's run passed over three such curves, and the two runs behind the ANSI X9.62 example curves passed over seven more (see figure). We do not know what criteria may have been used, or whether this was an unintentional artifact.

Because the number of skipped candidates is small, we do not believe it is plausible that weakened curves were selected. That would imply that weakened curves are common and easy to find. It is still conceivable that these curves were selected to have a specific property in principle by searching over timestamps to the random number generator. However, you would only need to do that if you were going to disclose the timestamp as some evidence that the seed was innocuously generated. Nothing in the numbers shows how many runs there were.

There is also one seed we were unable to recover. The fifth binary seed, B-163, fits nothing Claude has tried and remains unexplained. Finally, we don’t know how the base points for P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 were generated. The same goes for the NIST binary curves.

The $36,864 for finding the seeds will be donated to the Internet Security Research Group.

This work was conducted at Anthropic by John Wood, Henry de Valence, Ava Howell, Zack Voase, Lucy Sweet, Amir Omidi, Paul Crowley, Iain McGinniss, Nicholas Carlini, and Steve Weis.

We would like to posthumously recognize Jerry Solinas who took being labeled an “evil Internet meme” and the “Yo La Tengo of NSA bogeymen” with good humor. Also thanks to Filippo Valsorda for organizing the NIST Elliptic Curves Seeds Bounty.

items.author: speckx
items.content:
Our estimates of total economic coverage, and of patterns in coverage, all come from the initial list of 29 benchmarks we chose. This is not a complete or perfectly representative sample of the broader universe of unsaturated, public, agentic economic benchmarks. Any incomplete list will necessarily bias down estimates of economic coverage, and it is difficult to bound that bias. We want to stress, therefore, that these results are provisional. We will update them as we expand the initial benchmark list.

We also capped the number of included benchmarks in each job family in order to maximize breadth of coverage. We think this makes our estimate of economy-wide benchmark coverage more accurate, at the cost of biasing down our estimates of coverage in the most-benchmarked job families (e.g. software engineering).

By selecting for unsaturated benchmarks, we risk understating benchmark coverage on O*NET tasks which are easier for LLMs to complete. On the other hand, including saturated benchmarks would risk overstating benchmark coverage if saturation is downstream of lower task realism. The latter claim seems likely, given that benchmarks often overstate LLM performance in real-world deployments. We think that the bias from including saturated benchmarks would be greater than the bias from excluding them, but neither option is ideal.

Finally, while we outline our benchmark selection criteria in theBenchmark Index tab, several criteria (like “Economic Realism”) are difficult to formalize and introduce some subjectivity in our choices.

items.title: JPEG XL vs. AVIF for web use-cases
items.author: farlight
items.content:
JPEG XL has now landed in all major browsers, so I figured I'd take a closer look at what it's good/bad at compared to other formats.

I'll go into full detail, with examples and benchmarks, but for those of you who don't have the time, here are the headlines:

For lossy photos on the web, AVIF almost always produces smaller files than JPEG XL. At default effort settings, the best JPEG XL version is typically 15–25% larger than the equivalent AVIF. At maximum effort settings, the gap narrows a little, to typically 6–20%. There are outliers, where JPEG XL is close to, or even beats AVIF, so if you want the absolute best result for a particular image, it's worth trying both. See the F1 image for a typical example, and the weasel for an outlier.

The JPEG XL encoder matters a lot.jixel, a newer JPEG XL encoder, usually produces smaller files than libjxl, except when the image has detailed transparency. The people image is one example.

For screenshots and illustrations, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The equivalent JPEG XL is 30–90% larger at default effort settings, and 20–70% larger at maximum effort settings. Lossy AVIF handles these well - you don't need to use lossless formats unless you really need bit-exact results. See the screenshot and illustration examples.

For images with transparency, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The libjxl version is 31–44% larger at default effort settings, and 61–70% larger at maximum effort settings. jixel always encodes transparency losslessly, which makes its files 2–3x the size of AVIF's. See the data.

AVIF is generally faster to encode, and uses less memory, when you factor in file size. jixel is faster than AVIF and uses less memory, but its files are typically significantly larger, so AVIF is better on balance. See the F1 image for one example.

AVIF is faster to decode. JPEG XL typically takes 2–3x as long to decode at medium quality, but the gap narrows at very high qualities, where Chrome can sometimes decode JPEG XL faster. The people image is one example.

Higher effort settings are worth it for AVIF and jixel, but not libjxl. libjxl's higher efforts are much slower, use a lot more memory, and barely improve the result. Sometimes they produce larger files than the default effort. The screenshot is an example of this.

AVIF's 4:2:0 mode (half colour resolution) shouldn't be your default. It rarely reduces file size, and it makes higher qualities harder to reach. Although, it is quicker to encode and decode. Stick with 4:4:4 if you don't have time to check both. The F1 image is one example, and the screenshot is an exception.

Quality settings are reliable for all the encoders. With a single quality setting, the resulting quality varies a bit between images, but all the encoders vary in the same direction, and in ways that seem reasonable. See the data.

Progressive JPEG XL is basically free at high effort. jixel recently added support for early progressive previews, and at its slowest setting they cost little or nothing, but at its default setting the files are 12% bigger. Firefox and Chrome support progressive JPEG XL. Safari still renders the final image, but doesn't show progressive previews. However, is this type of progressive rendering a good user experience? See the examples and data.

AVIF supports progressive rendering! It's Chrome-only for now, but it's in progress for Firefox. It's more complex than progressive JPEG XL, but it gives you more control over what the preview looks like, the files are usually smaller, and they're much faster to decode. See for yourself.

For HDR, JPEG XL lacks gain maps, which is a significant limitation compared to AVIF. The JPEG XL format supports gain maps, but they aren't supported by browser decoders, and the encoding story is messy/experimental. When comparing non-gain mapped HDR content, the two quality metrics I used disagree a lot, but they agree that JPEG XL produces smaller files compared to AVIF. See the examples.

JPEG XL can make existing JPEGs 9–20% smaller, without further loss. It's also as fast or faster to decode, except for small images. See the data.

For lossless, JPEG XL is the clear winner. Lossless WebP is 9–17% larger for photos, and lossless AVIF is 30–120% larger. But lossless images are almost never what you want on the web. If you do use them on the web (like I do on this page), watch out for jixel's higher efforts - it often produces files that are too slow to decode. See the data.

Animated image formats continue to be a dumb idea. Please don't use them. Learn more, if you must.

For web use-cases, I'd currently default to AVIF 4:4:4, with the highest effort level I can be bothered with. If I felt AVIF was producing an unusually large file, I'd take a look at JPEG XL via jixel, and see if it did better.

Both AVIF and JPEG XL (via jixel) have seen massive improvements recently, so it's possible that this recommendation could change in future. There's been a lot of misinformation around this stuff, and your AI will happily deliver that misinformation to you. Instead, test things with your own images.

AVIF folks suggest that JPEG XL is technically limited compared to AVIF. That might be true, but in this article I'm focusing on results with today's implementations.

I 'created' a benchmarking script, that encodes images using various codecs at various settings, and records various details.

I'm using the latest released versions of the image codecs, which at time of writing is:

  • libjxl 0.12.0 (using its encoder)
  • jixel 0.4.2 (git ), a second JPEG XL encoder
  • cwebp 1.6.0 (lossless WebP is used later in the article)

I chose a selection of images, and encoded most of them to a width of 1598 pixels - which is 2x the maximum width images appear on this blog. This means they look sharp on high density displays, which most users have. As a result, if you're viewing this on a small or low density screen, you're not getting the full experience.

I ran these benchmarks on my 2024 MacBook Pro (M4 Pro).

I encoded the image at various codec qualities, and chose versions that were closest to particular SSIMULACRA2 scores - a perceptual image quality metric by the folks behind JPEG XL. 50 is considered medium quality, 70 high, 80 very high, and 90 visually lossless. Although, I'm not sure if these ratings take high density displays into account.

Throughout the article, the visual comparisons, like above, use each encoder's maximum effort, except in cases where maximum effort results in a larger file (yes, that happens).

For archival, I'd tend towards near-lossless qualities, but if I'm just displaying an illustrative image on my blog, performance is more important to me. I'm personally happy with the 70 result above. If you zoom in, you can see the quality loss, but if I was really concerned about the zoom-in case, I'd use something like the API to load in a higher resolution image when that happens, rather than make the download bigger for everyone.

At lower qualities you can see the difference in strategy between the codecs. The detail loss is around the same, but AVIF tends to smooth things out compared to the original, whereas JPEG XL seems to introduce rougher patterns.

Also, I feel that, at medium quality (50), the AVIF and libjxl look better than the jixel version. The jixel version has a lot of visible noise around the BWT logo, and the Microsoft text on the front wing is way less legible. It makes me wonder about the metric a bit.

Anyway, here's my interpretation of the results:

  • At default efforts, the best JPEG XL image is 14–17% larger than the AVIF image for the same quality. jixel is the better JPEG XL encoder at medium/high quality, and libjxl is slightly better at very high quality. At maximum efforts, the best JPEG XL image (jixel 'extraslow') is 6–15% larger than AVIF (s0).
  • jixel at its slowest setting slightly beats AVIF's default effort, with files 1–10% smaller. The biggest gain is at very high quality.
  • At default efforts, jixel is 12–36% faster than AVIF, but its files are 14–18% larger. To match the file size of AVIF's default, jixel needs its 'extraslow' setting, which takes 18–27x as long as AVIF. libjxl's default takes 1.5–2x as long as AVIF's default, and still produces bigger files.
  • At default efforts, jixel uses around half the memory of AVIF, but again, its files are 14–18% larger. To match the file size of AVIF's default, jixel 'extraslow' uses ~10x the memory. libjxl's default uses 2–3x the memory of AVIF, and its higher efforts use ~7x.
  • JPEG XL takes 2–3x as long to decode at medium quality, narrowing to ~1.5–1.8x at very high quality. Safari's JPEG XL decoder is the slowest.
  • Higher effort is worth it for AVIF. AVIF's s5 gets you ~10% smaller files for ~3x the encode time.
  • Higher effort is worth it for jixel too, up to 'slow'. 'slow' gets you 9–13% smaller files than its default 'fast', for ~3.7x the encode time. 'extraslow' saves another 3–8%, but takes ~8x longer than 'slow' and uses ~9x the memory. Even so, AVIF still wins when given the same encode time: AVIF s5 takes about as long as jixel 'slow', and its files are ~13% smaller.
  • Higher effort isn't worth it for libjxl. libjxl's maximum effort is barely any better than its default, but takes ~18x longer.
  • AVIF's 4:2:0 mode doesn't help much. It's slightly faster to encode/decode, and uses less memory, but the files aren't meaningfully smaller, and it struggles to reach higher qualities.

Here's the full data, so you can make up your own mind:

I've heard people say that AVIF's tendency to smooth out details makes it bad for human faces, so I picked this image from Unsplash.

The results of the benchmark for this image:

  • At default efforts, the best JPEG XL image is 17–24% larger than the AVIF image for the same quality. jixel is the better JPEG XL encoder across the whole quality range this time. libjxl is 30–50% larger than AVIF, which is a much bigger gap than the F1 image. At maximum efforts, the best JPEG XL image (jixel 'extraslow') is 12–17% larger than AVIF (s0).
  • jixel at its slowest setting doesn't quite match AVIF's default effort this time. It's a few percent larger at medium/high quality, and only edges ahead at very high quality.
  • At default efforts, jixel is 18–33% faster than AVIF, but its files are 17–24% larger. Even jixel's 'extraslow' setting, which takes 25–39x as long as AVIF, only matches AVIF's default file size at very high quality. libjxl's default takes 1.5–2.2x as long as AVIF's default, and still produces bigger files.
  • At default efforts, jixel uses around half the memory of AVIF, but again, its files are 17–24% larger. jixel 'extraslow' gets closest to AVIF's default file size, but uses ~10x the memory. libjxl's default uses 2–3.3x the memory of AVIF, and its higher efforts use ~7x.
  • JPEG XL takes 2–2.9x as long to decode at medium quality, narrowing to ~1.3–1.7x at very high quality. At the very top of the quality range, libjxl images decode as fast as AVIF in Chrome, but not in the other browsers.
  • Higher effort is worth it for AVIF. AVIF's s5 gets you 5–8% smaller files for ~3x the encode time. That's a smaller gain than the F1 image.
  • Higher effort is worth it for jixel too, up to 'slow'. 'slow' gets you 7–14% smaller files than its default 'fast', for ~3.9x the encode time. 'extraslow' saves another 4–6%, but takes ~10x longer than 'slow' and uses ~9x the memory. AVIF still wins when given the same encode time: AVIF s5 takes about as long as jixel 'slow', and its files are 8–17% smaller.
  • Higher effort is somewhat worth it for libjxl on this image. Unlike the F1 image, libjxl's maximum effort gets you 4–11% smaller files than its default. But it takes ~10x longer, and it still produces much bigger files than AVIF at its default effort.
  • AVIF's 4:2:0 mode doesn't help much. Same as the F1 image. ColorVideoVDP gives it a small (~4%) advantage, but SSIMULACRA2 doesn't.

At lower qualities, you can see the smoothing on the face, but it's the same for both AVIF and JPEG XL.

Both AVIF and JPEG XL are capable of showing something progressively as the image loads. Chrome and Firefox support progressive JPEG XL, whereas only Chrome supports progressive AVIF. This is the 18 megapixel image again, so if you're viewing this on a device with a smaller screen, you're not getting the full effect.

Progressive AVIF and JPEG XL work very differently. With JPEG XL, you can opt into the data being stored in such a way that a decoder can render low resolution versions, before it brings in the higher resolution tiles. jixel recently (like, yesterday at time of writing) added support for this too. It's called "progressive DC", and it's the most important kind of progressive rendering for JPEG XL.

With AVIF, progressions work more like frames of a video. You provide up to four frames, so that's three phases before the final image. Again, like a video, each frame can use data from the previous frame as an optimisation. An advantage of this is you can choose exactly how those frames look. In the example above, I went with a single preview frame: a 1/8th resolution version, with a bit of blurring. But, your preview frames can be completely different images if you really want.

There's a lack of data when it comes to progressive images and user experience, so these are just my reckons:

If you're on a bad connection, data doesn't arrive gradually like some throttling tools will have you believe. It tends to come in bursts. So, there's little benefit to progressive rendering on smaller images, and I'm not sure that many progressive phases is particularly useful.

I think that it's nice to have a preview for images that may take some time to load. I've experienced this personally, where a site or app has given me something clearly not-loaded, but with enough detail to know what's coming. That's useful to me, as I can decide things like, if it's worth waiting for the whole thing. This is also why I think things like BlurHash are cute, but useless. They're not a preview, so there's little a user can do with the information provided.

The preview frame I chose for the AVIF is enough to tell it's an open-wheel race car. If you know F1, you'll know what team it is. You might even know where the photo was taken. And it delivers that in ~11.5 kB.

The JPEG XL gets a BlurHash-like preview on screen in ~2 kB, but it takes until ~63 kB to match the preview quality of the AVIF. After that, it continues to improve gradually, providing a more detailed and higher quality image as more data arrives.

However, I'm not convinced this is a good user experience, as it presents the user with something they may mistake for fully-loaded, but poor quality. For example:

Here's a crop of the JPEG XL, 80% loaded. It seems reasonable that someone would look at that, and just assume I took the picture badly, leaving parts out of focus. You could probably convince me that blurring the ApeCoin logo is a societal benefit, but it still feels like a suboptimal user experience.

AVIF's system gives me more control, but it's also more complex.

Let's get back to lossy compression, but this time HDR! There are a few ways to encode HDR images, and we're going to look at two.

(PQ) tells each pixel what to be. Each value maps to an absolute brightness, up to 10,000 nits, with the curve shaped so the data is spent where our eyes are most sensitive. If the image asks for colours and brightnesses the display can't show (no consumer display can hit 10,000 nits), the browser/OS has to tone-map it down, and how well that's done varies between platforms.

are different. The main image is a regular SDR image (usually), and alongside it is a 'gain map', which applies a brightness and colour change to each pixel to achieve the HDR version.

  1. The same image will look exactly as you want on an SDR display - the gain map is simply ignored.
  2. If the display supports HDR, but maybe not as much as the image needs (for example, the screen is at low or maximum brightness), the browser/OS can apply as much of the gain map as it can handle.

CSS and let us serve an SDR or PQ image to the user via the media query, but then you're relying on tone mapping in cases where the browser signals HDR support, but it doesn't support the full range.

Although the JPEG XL format supports gain maps, no browser handles them, and the encoding story is messy.

AVIF supports gain maps, and you encode them by providing two images: the SDR image and the HDR image. It uses those to calculate and encode the gain map.

Your browser/screen doesn't support HDR, so the PQ images will look bad.

At medium brightnesses, on an HDR screen, the gain map and PQ images look the same. At maximum brightnesses, on my Pixel 10 Pro and 2024 MacBook Pro, the PQ images get a bit blown out, and the gain map image looks better. At low brightness on my Pixel 10 Pro, again the gain map image looks better.

This is because, at extreme brightness levels, the device doesn't have the full HDR headroom to display the image, and gain maps can handle these cases better. So, although gain maps seem to add a lot to the file size, I think it's worth it.

Maybe there's a future where tone mapping gets much better, and the advantage of a gain map becomes less significant.

JPEG XL allows you to convert an existing JPEG to JPEG XL without additional loss. I tested this with the F1 image at a range of sizes and JPEG qualities:

  • The JPEG XL is 9–20% smaller than the JPEG. The saving grows with resolution, from ~9% at 400 pixels wide to ~20% at 4,900 pixels wide. The saving is slightly smaller at higher JPEG qualities. libjxl and jixel produce practically identical file sizes.
  • For small images, JPEG XL is slower to decode than JPEG, taking 1.4–2.7x as long, depending on the browser. But it's just a millisecond or two.
  • For larger images, JPEG XL is faster to decode in Chrome and Safari. From ~1,000 pixels wide, it matches JPEG, and at the largest sizes, it decodes in around half the time. In Firefox, it ends up around the same speed as JPEG.
  • jixel's output is slightly slower to decode than libjxl's in Chrome and Firefox, by up to ~25%. But again, these are small numbers, at most a few milliseconds.

Of course, if you have the original, you'd be way better off creating a proper new lossy version with AVIF or JPEG XL, but it's pretty cool that the JPEGs end up smaller, and sometimes faster to decode. Although, I suppose this is just pointing to a missing optimisation in browser JPEG decoders.

At highest efforts, libjxl and jixel are within a few percent of each other, WebP is 5–44% larger, and AVIF is 29–176% larger.
  • Encode time: . libjxl's default takes 0.1–0.5 seconds, which is faster than WebP's default, and similar to AVIF's default, while producing smaller files than both.
  • Encode memory: or , depending on the image. WebP's default uses around half the memory of libjxl's default (55–110 MB vs 110–250 MB), but libjxl's files are smaller. For photos, WebP can't match libjxl's default file size even at its maximum effort, which uses more memory than libjxl's default. For the screenshot, they use around the same memory, but libjxl's file is smaller. The illustration is the exception: WebP's maximum effort produces a file 20% smaller than libjxl's default, using the same memory.
  • Decode time: or , depending on the image. WebP decodes photos in 17–39 ms in all browsers, and the screenshot in ~5 ms. libjxl's output takes 1–2.2x as long in Chrome, 1.4–2.7x as long in Firefox, and 2.1–3.2x as long in Safari. But for photos, JPEG XL's smaller files more than make up for this on a first load, unless the connection is really fast. For the screenshot and illustration, WebP's decode advantage wins. Lossless AVIF is particularly slow to decode, taking up to 4x as long as libjxl's output in Chrome.
  • It's significantly larger than the others, and slower to decode.
  • jixel's 'medium' setting is the sweet spot for file size. It beats libjxl's default on every image (0.5–23% smaller), and is within 2–3% of the best result for photos, taking 0.4–0.7 seconds. But it uses 470–670 MB of memory, and its output is slower to decode than libjxl's, particularly in Safari.
  • jixel's 'slow' and 'extraslow' output is very slow to decode for photos. ~200–290 ms, compared to 22–95 ms for libjxl's output. That's 2–13x slower, depending on the browser. It's also slow for the alpha image, at 80–123 ms compared to 14–27 ms for libjxl's output. This doesn't happen with the screenshot and illustration. This means, for my use-case on this page, I'd avoid it.
  • libjxl's maximum effort is very slow. It produces files 2–7% smaller than its default for photos, and ~25% smaller for the screenshot and illustration, but takes 9–46 seconds, which is 50–180x as long as its default. jixel gets the same results in a couple of seconds.
  • jixel's default 'fast' setting isn't great for lossless. It's the fastest encoder by far (40–80 ms), but its files are 16–32% larger than libjxl's default for photos, and ~80% larger for the screenshot and illustration.
  • jixel's patches feature helps a bit with the screenshot (4–9% smaller), but makes no difference to the illustration.

Animated image formats are dumb and animated JPEG XL is no exception. Video formats are better at video. They're built for it. They're optimised for it. Not just in terms of encoding, but also in terms of playback.

I encoded a short clip, and the animated AVIF was 725 kB, and the JPEG XL was 2.17 MB for the same ColorVideoVDP score (9.5).

The JPEG XL is super noisy compared to the AVIF, because each frame is encoded individually, and arttifacts land in different places per frame.

AVIF is basically the keyframe format of AV1 video, with a bunch of still-image-specific optimisations thrown in. Animated AVIF however, is pretty much just a repackaging of AV1 video. You can convert an AV1 MP4 to AVIF and back losslessly - it's just a container change. That's why it performs so much better, because it's built for motion.

However, animated AVIF plays like shit in Chrome and Safari. It's fine in Firefox, so this is purely an implementation problem. But… is right there.

No, I'm not adding a demo. I don't want it on my server. Use video formats for video.

I already gave you my conclusions at the start, so I guess I'm ready to hit publish.

I'm a little nervous about this, because discourse around JPEG XL can get a little… weird. I see a lot of conspiracy theories about Google trying to 'silence' JPEG XL, even though one of the leads of the project worked at Google, as part of a team that were working on JPEG XL. That same leader claimed that the post-COVID layoffs wouldn't have happened if companies simply used JPEG XL. I was recently called a racist for asking about JPEG XL use-cases. This kind of thing just doesn't happen with other technologies and standards I follow. So, urm, I'm kinda bracing for impact here.

My first version of this article was very negative about JPEG XL, but then I heard about jixel, and honestly, I'm really excited about it. There's serious competition between AVIF and JPEG XL now, and whoever wins, we'll all benefit from better image compression.

Waymo is officially heading to Canada! We’re laying the groundwork for our fully autonomous ride-hailing service in Toronto, investing in local facilities and jobs, with the goal of welcoming our first riders in 2028.

In the coming days, you’ll start to see Waymo vehicles on the streets of Toronto as we begin driving manually. We are taking a rigorous, phased, safety-first approach starting with high-definition mapping of local street networks and testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel. This validation period will ensure the Waymo Driver adapts seamlessly to Toronto’s distinct driving conditions.

“Expanding into Canada marks an important milestone in Waymo’s global journey,” said Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana.“Toronto is one of the world’s great cities — innovative, diverse, and forward-looking. We’re proud to bring the Waymo Driver to Canada’s largest city and to partner with the vibrant business, arts and cultural communities that share our commitment to safer streets and more accessible mobility.”

To serve Toronto, we’re partnering with Element Fleet Management, a Toronto-headquartered company and global leader in intelligent fleet and mobility solutions that will provide end-to-end fleet management services. Together with Element and our partners, we’ll invest in hundreds of roles over time spanning fleet maintenance, validation driving, customer service, and other operations functions that support our service. This deep partnership builds on Waymo’s existing ties to Canada, which includes our long-term investor relationship with the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and our manufacturing partner, Magna International.

"As a Canadian company, we are proud to be expanding our partnership with Waymo to help bring autonomous ride-hailing to Toronto,” said Laura Dottori-Attanasio, Chief Executive Officer, Element Fleet Management. Together with Waymo, Element will help create employment opportunities providing the fleet expertise, operational capabilities, and intelligent mobility solutions needed to support autonomous fleets reliably and at scale."

As one of North America’s fastest-growing metropolitan regions, Toronto has both evolving mobility demands and a dynamic and growing number of tools. From bike lanes to public transit, Waymo’s all-weather Driver can provide an additional option that complements the city’s transportation ecosystem. The data from over 400 million fully autonomous kilometres driven shows the Waymo Driver was involved in 95% fewer (20x fewer) crashes involving serious injury or worse compared to humans in the cities where we operate.

Safety and accessibility are fundamental to Waymo's mission to be the world's most trusted driver, and we're proud to collaborate with leading accessibility and mobility advocacy organizations, including BALANCE for Blind Adults, CNIB, Community Living Toronto, Connected Canadians, and Epilepsy Ontario, among others.

“Innovation that removes barriers to independence is at the heart of everything we do. Waymo’s history of partnering with the sight loss community to build accessible solutions is encouraging and their decision to engage with us early reflects the kind of approach that leads to real results,” said Michelle McQuigge, CEO, BALANCE for Blind Adults.

We can't wait to help residents and visitors explore everything Toronto has to offer. If you’re ready to experience Waymo in Toronto, please sign up for updates to be among the first to ride when we’re ready: waymo.com/waymo-in-canada.

Waymo arrive officiellement au Canada ! Nous préparons le lancement de notre service de transport par véhicules autonomes à Toronto. Nous investissons dans les infrastructures locales et dans la création d’emplois en vue d’accueillir nos premiers passagers en 2028.

Nous sommes fiers d’introduire le Waymo Driver dans la plus grande ville du Canada et de collaborer avec les communautés dynamiques des affaires, des arts et de la culture qui partagent notre engagement envers des rues plus sécuritaires et une mobilité plus accessible. »

Pour assurer notre service à Toronto, nous faisons équipe avec Element Fleet Management, une entreprise dont le siège social se trouve à Toronto et qui est un leader mondial des solutions intelligentes de gestion de flottes et de mobilité. Ce partenariat s’inscrit dans la continuité des liens que Waymo a déjà tissés avec le Canada, notamment avec l’Office d’investissement du régime de pensions du Canada (Investissements RPC), un investisseur de longue date, et Magna International, son partenaire manufacturier.

Toronto figure parmi les régions métropolitaines dont la croissance est la plus rapide en Amérique du Nord. Les besoins en matière de mobilité y évoluent et les options de transport se multiplient. Des pistes cyclables au transport en commun, le Waymo Driver, conçu pour fonctionner par tous les temps, pourrait offrir une option supplémentaire en complément des moyens de transport existants. Selon les données recueillies sur plus de 400 millions de kilomètres parcourus en conduite entièrement autonome, les véhicules Waymo ont été impliqués dans 95 % moins d’accidents entraînant des blessures graves ou plus graves que les véhicules conduits par des humains dans les villes où le service est offert.
